1.note: The expression **was restrained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he could not move about freely] or [he kept himself hidden]

The author is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of Saul] or [because Saul was trying to kill him]

The author is using the possessive form to describe warriors who were **helpers** to David when he fought a **battle**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they were among the warriors who helped him fight battles]

2.note: When archers draw an arrow back and look down its length to aim it, they hold their mouth next to their hand, so they appear to be kissing the bowstring. The author is using this action to represent the entire use of a bow in battle, especially shooting arrows at enemy soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Skillful archers]
See how you translated the term “brother” in 6:39. Alternate translation: [from the kinsmen of Saul]
See how you translated the name “Israel” in [9:1](ta:09). Alternate translation: [from the descendants of Benjamin] or [from the tribe of Benjamin]

3.note: To translate the term **head** here and in verses 9, 14, 18, and 23, see how you translated it in 11:20. Alternate translation: [The commander]

4.note: This could mean: (1) that **Ishmaiah** was equal to the members of the **Thirty** in terms of his military prowess and that he was in fact a greater warrior than the typical member. Alternate translation: [who was as great as David’s 30 greatest warriors and greater than the typical one] or (2) that **Ishmaiah** was a member and the commander of the **Thirty** at this time, but not at the later time when the list in 11:10–47 was drawn up (since his name does not appear there; some interpreters suggest that he may have died in the meantime). Alternate translation: [a member and the commander at this time of the group of David’s 30 greatest warriors]

6.note: While verses 2–7 list members of the tribe of Benjamin who came to David, the term **Korahites** seems to refer to one of the clans of the tribe of Levi, particularly since **Elkanah** and **Isshiah** were common Levite names. The Levites did live among the various Israelite tribes, and interpreters suggest that these were Levites living within the territory of Benjamin who came as warriors with the Benjaminites listed in these verses. Alternate translation: [Levites from the clan of Korah living among the Benjaminites]

8.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Gadite**. He means the Gadites (the members of the tribe of Gad) in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And from the Gadites]

The author is speaking as if these Gadite warriors actually had **faces of lions**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and their faces were very fierce, as lions’ faces are]

The author is using the facial appearance of these warriors to represent their entire character as warriors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to do that.

The point of this comparison is that just as **gazelles** can run very fast, so these warriors could run very fast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they were very fast, as gazelles on the hills are, when it came to running]

9.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second** or **third**, you could represent these numbers in a form that your language would use. You can do the same with the numbers in verses 10–13. Alternate translation: [Obadiah, number two; Eliab, number three] or [Obadiah, the next; Eliab, after him]

14.note: As an overstatement for emphasis, the author is saying that the **least** of these Gadite soldiers could defeat **100** opponents in battle, and the **greatest** of them could defeat **1,000** opponents in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [They were such good soldiers that even the least of them could defeat many opponents in battle, and the greatest of them could defeat very many opponents in battle]

15.note: The **first month** of the Hebrew year was in the spring. As the rest of the verse indicates, at this time, the Jordan River was at flood stage because of melting snow in the mountains. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the spring when the snow was melting]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of the valleys were made to flee]

The author is speaking the **valleys** on the **east** and **west** sides of the Jordan as if they were living things that were able to **flee**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the water entirely covered the river valleys]

17.note: The author is using **to their faces** as a common expression of the culture to mean “into their presence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to meet with them personally]

Here the author is using **answered** to express that David was responding to the arrival of these men rather than to something that they had said to him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and in response to their arrival, he said to them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peacefully]

Here David is using his **heart** to represent his feelings and inclinations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will be happy to have unity with you]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [But if you have come to betray me]

Here, the **palms**, part of a person’s hands, represent that person’s actions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even though I have not committed any violence]

David is saying what he wants God to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech, and follow the decision you have made as a team about how speakers will express in such contexts what they want someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that the God of our fathers will see what you are doing and judge you]

18.note: The author is speaking as if God’s **Spirit** actually **wore** Amasai as if he had been a garment. He means that the Spirit inspired Amasai and gave him the confidence to say what he said. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the Spirit inspired Amasai]
If it would be helpful to your readers, here you could use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [the Thirty, and he said, “For you, David]

The expression **the Thirty** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. (They seem to have recommended this because **Amasai** is not listed among the Thirty in 11:10–47.) You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the captains]

If **the Thirty** is the correct reading, then the author would be assuming that readers would understand that he means Amasai was the **head of the Thirty** at this time, but not at the later time when the list in chapter 11 was compiled. (Some interpreters suggest that he may have died in the meantime.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if you decide not to use the alternative reading “captains.” Alternate translation: [the Thirty at this time]

Amasai is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [We are for you, David, and we are with you, son of Jesse]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [We are for you, David! Yes, we are with you, son of Jesse]

18.q: שָׁל֨וֹם ׀ שָׁל֜וֹם לְ⁠ךָ֗ וְ⁠שָׁלוֹם֙ לְ⁠עֹ֣זְרֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֥י עֲזָרְ⁠ךָ֖ אֱלֹהֶ֑י⁠ךָ
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since your God helps you, peace, peace to you, and peace to the one helping you]
See how you translated the term “peace” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [May you be very peaceful, and may the one helping you be peaceful]

Amasai is repeating the word **peace** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Great peace to you]

19.note: The author is using the term **fell** a common expression of the culture that describes changing loyalty from one master to another. Alternate translation: [And some from Manasseh came over to David] or [And some from Manasseh became loyal to David]

The author assumes that readers will understand that he is referring to the events described in 1 Samuel 28:1–2 and 1 Samuel 29:1–11. You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

19.q: וְ⁠לֹ֣א עֲזָרֻ֑⁠ם כִּ֣י בְ⁠עֵצָ֗ה שִׁלְּחֻ֜⁠הוּ סַרְנֵ֤י פְלִשְׁתִּים֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר בְּ⁠רָאשֵׁ֕י⁠נוּ יִפּ֖וֹל אֶל־אֲדֹנָ֥י⁠ו שָׁאֽוּל
19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But since by counsel the lords of the Philistines sent him away, saying, “By our heads, he will fall to his master Saul,” they did not help them]

The pronoun **they** refers to David and his men, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Philistines. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But David and his men did not help the Philistines]

The author is using the term **saying** to introduce a direct quotation, but this is something that the **lords of the Philistines** said to each other when they took **counsel** together, as 1 Samuel 29:4–5 describes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [saying to each other]

The lords of the Philistines are concerned that, following a warfare practice of the time, David will kill some of their soldiers, cut off their heads, and present them to Saul as proof of his loyalty. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [By killing our soldiers, cutting of their heads, and presenting them as proof of loyalty]

By **our**, the lords who are speaking mean to include both themselves and those to whom they are speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction. (They do not necessarily mean themselves personally, but they do mean their own soldiers and commanders.)
See how you translated the term **fell** earlier in this verse. Alternate translation: [he will defect]

20.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [When David went]
See how you translated the term “fell” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [the following men became loyal to him]

This could mean: (1) that these men were leaders of clans. In Hebrew, the term “thousand” can mean a “clan.” Alternate translation: [leaders of clans] or (2) that these men were commanders of groups of about a thousand soldiers. Alternate translation: [commanders of groups of a thousand soldiers]

21.q: וְ⁠הֵ֗מָּה עָזְר֤וּ עִם־דָּוִיד֙ עַֽל־הַ⁠גְּד֔וּד כִּֽי־גִבּ֥וֹרֵי חַ֖יִל כֻּלָּ֑⁠ם
21.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since all of them were warriors of valor, they, they helped with David against the troop]

The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they helped** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of these men in helping David at a difficult time. The sense is that they arrived just when they were needed and willingly did what they could to help. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And they were able to help]
It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [they helped David]

The author assumes that readers will understand that he is referring to the events described in 1 Samuel 30:1–20. You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers, and you could give some indication of these events in the text of your translation. Alternate translation: [to defeat the band of Amalekites that had raided Ziklag and to recover the people and possessions they had taken]

22.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. The author means that these men from Manasseh coming to David is understandable in light of the fact that many soldiers were continually coming to David at this time. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that soldiers came to David continually. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [day after day] or [practically every day]
The pronoun **they** refers to soldiers from various tribes of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israelite soldiers were coming]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [until they amounted to a great camp]

Here, a **camp** represents an “army,” since an army stays in a camp when it is fighting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to a great army, like an army of God]

The author is using **of God** as a common expression of his culture to mean “very great.” (Compare, for example, 1 Samuel 14:15, “a trembling of God.”) He is comparing the soldiers who gathered around David to the kind of huge army that a king would lead. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [like the huge army of a kingdom]

23.note: The expression **equipped** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the heads who had equipped themselves for war] or [the heads who were capable of fighting in war]

The author is using one part of these soldiers, their **heads**, to mean all of them in the act of coming to David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the soldiers who had equipped themselves for war] or [the soldiers who were capable of fighting in war]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:14. Alternate translation: [to make him rule the kingdom instead of Saul]

The author is using Yahweh’s **mouth** to represent what he said by using his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh had said]

24.note: The author is not referring to a specific **shield** or **spear**. He means those weapons in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [carriers of shields and spears] or [soldiers armed with shields and spears]
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:23. Alternate translation: [soldiers who were capable of fighting in war]

29.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:2. Alternate translation: [the kinsmen of Saul]

The author is using **keeping the keeping** as a common expression of his culture to mean that most of the Benjaminites had been supporting Saul. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [had been maintaining their allegiance to] or [had been defending the interests of]

The author is speaking as if Saul’s royal dynasty, and specifically at this time the reign of his son Ish Bosheth, as if it had actually been a **house**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dynasty of Saul] or [the reign of Saul’s son Ish Bosheth]

30.note: See how you translated the same expression in 5:24. Alternate translation: [men with great reputations]

31.note: The expression **were designated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whose leaders designated them]

32.note: The author is using the term **times** to mean “circumstances” or “situations,” since those come about at certain times. Alternate translation: [knowers of understanding of situations]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [knowers of times] or [discerners of situations]

The author means that being **knowers … of times** enabled these men **to know** what to do in the situation. It may be more natural in your language to use a different kind of verbal expression. Alternate translation: [who knew what Israel should do]
See how you translated the term **Israel** in 2:7. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]
See how you translated the term “brothers” in 6:39. Alternate translation: [their kinsmen]

The author is using the term **mouth** to represent the commands that these **heads** or commanders would give by using their mouths. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under their command]

33.note: The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [with many different military weapons]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and inclinations. This expression means that these 50,000 soldiers were able to **keep rank** because none of them felt somewhat brave but also somewhat afraid or somewhat committed to fighting but also somewhat hesitant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [without being double-minded] or [with complete commitment]

34.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:24. Alternate translation: [with shields and spears]

35.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Danite**. He means the members of that clan in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And from the Danites]

37.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 12:35. Alternate translation: [from the Reubenites and the Gadites]
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:33. Alternate translation: [with many different military weapons]

38.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s desires and intentions. The expression **with a whole heart** means that these men desired exclusively to **make David reign**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [wholeheartedly] or [with sincere determination]

The author is saying **all** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the other Israelites]
Here the **heart** once again represents people’s desires and intentions. Alternate translation: [had an identical desire]

39.q: וַ⁠יִּהְיוּ־שָׁ֤ם עִם־דָּוִיד֙ יָמִ֣ים שְׁלוֹשָׁ֔ה אֹכְלִ֖ים וְ⁠שׁוֹתִ֑ים כִּֽי־הֵכִ֥ינוּ לָ⁠הֶ֖ם אֲחֵי⁠הֶֽם
39.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since their brothers had prepared for them, they were there with David three days eating and drinking]
See how you translated the term “brothers” in 12:32. Alternate translation: [their kinsmen] or [their fellow Israelites]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [had prepared food and drink for them]

40.q: וְ⁠גַ֣ם הַ⁠קְּרֽוֹבִים־אֲ֠לֵי⁠הֶם עַד־יִשָׂשכָ֨ר וּ⁠זְבֻל֜וּן וְ⁠נַפְתָּלִ֗י מְבִיאִ֣ים לֶ֡חֶם בַּ⁠חֲמוֹרִ֣ים וּ⁠בַ⁠גְּמַלִּ֣ים וּ⁠בַ⁠פְּרָדִ֣ים ׀ וּֽ⁠בַ⁠בָּקָ֡ר מַאֲכָ֡ל קֶ֠מַח דְּבֵלִ֨ים וְ⁠צִמּוּקִ֧ים וְ⁠יַֽיִן־וְ⁠שֶׁ֛מֶן וּ⁠בָקָ֥ר וְ⁠צֹ֖אן לָ⁠רֹ֑ב כִּ֥י שִׂמְחָ֖ה בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
40.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And also, because joy was in Israel, the ones near to them, unto Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, were bringing bread on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen: food of flour, fig cakes and raisins cakes and wine and oil and oxen and sheep in abundance]

The author is referring to all of the Israelites by naming two extremes, **the ones near** to Hebron and the ones living faraway in the territories of **Issachar**, **Zebulun**, and **Naphtali**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And also people from throughout Israel]
The author is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food]
